frictionVectors.title: European energy dependence
frictionVectors.details: Europe relies on Algerian pipeline and LNG supplies, giving Algiers leverage but also exposing it to pressure over volumes, pricing, and migration cooperation.

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara and regional rivalry
frictionVectors.details: Algeria's support for Sahrawi self-determination sustains strategic tension with Morocco, complicating Maghreb trade, energy integration, and infrastructure connectivity.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign oil dependence
frictionVectors.details: International operators, offshore technology, and external financing remain essential to Angola's petroleum output, limiting effective domestic control despite state participation.

frictionVectors.title: Lobito Corridor competition
frictionVectors.details: The corridor is attracting Western and Gulf-backed investment because of its access to Central African minerals, creating strategic leverage but also pressure over ownership, security, and export priorities.

frictionVectors.title: Regional trade vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Benin's port and transit economy remains exposed to Nigerian policy shifts, Sahel instability, and disruptions affecting access to northern markets.

frictionVectors.title: External security dependence
frictionVectors.details: Growing jihadist threats near the northern border are increasing reliance on foreign training, intelligence, and security assistance, constraining autonomous resource and infrastructure planning.

frictionVectors.title: Diamond market concentration
frictionVectors.details: Botswana retains strong negotiating capacity with major diamond firms, but global demand shifts and synthetic stones threaten fiscal revenues and the country's primary resource base.

frictionVectors.title: Critical minerals competition
frictionVectors.details: Foreign interest in copper, nickel, and other minerals is increasing, requiring Botswana to balance investment access with local processing, environmental safeguards, and national ownership.

frictionVectors.title: Gold-sector renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The government is seeking greater state control and domestic value capture from gold mining, creating friction with multinational operators over permits, taxes, and operating conditions.

frictionVectors.title: Russian security partnership
frictionVectors.details: Expanded reliance on Russian military support is reducing dependence on Western partners but introduces uncertainty over costs, accountability, and the protection of mining and transport infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Opaque mining and foreign capital
frictionVectors.details: Gold, nickel and rare-earth prospects attract Gulf, Chinese and regional interests, while weak oversight limits Burundi's ability to capture full value. The government is seeking greater state participation but lacks infrastructure and regulatory capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Rwanda border and Lake Tanganyika security
frictionVectors.details: Relations with Rwanda remain strained over armed groups and mutual accusations, complicating trade routes and security cooperation. Control of Lake Tanganyika transport and fisheries is also vulnerable to regional instability.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic port and maritime competition
frictionVectors.details: Mindelo and other maritime assets attract European, American and Chinese interest because of Cabo Verde's Atlantic position. Praia generally preserves policy autonomy, but infrastructure financing can create long-term external dependence.

frictionVectors.title: Tourism and energy vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Heavy reliance on imported fuel, tourism and remittances leaves the economy exposed to external shocks. Renewable-energy expansion improves resilience but remains dependent on foreign finance and technology.

highlights: Oil, gas and minerals remain externally exposed

frictionVectors.title: Chinese infrastructure and resource access
frictionVectors.details: Chinese firms remain important in roads, rail, ports and extractive projects, giving Beijing substantial commercial leverage over strategic infrastructure. Debt, project opacity and limited domestic processing constrain Cameroon's sovereign return.

frictionVectors.title: Anglophone conflict and border insecurity
frictionVectors.details: The northwest and southwest conflicts continue to disrupt agriculture, transport and local resource governance. Instability near Nigeria and the Central African Republic further raises security costs around major corridors and extractive zones.

frictionVectors.title: Russian security-for-resources model
frictionVectors.details: Russian-linked security personnel and political networks retain major influence over regime protection and mining access. Weak oversight and opaque concessions limit state revenue and deepen dependence on an external patron.

frictionVectors.title: Corridor insecurity and regional dependence
frictionVectors.details: Armed-group activity and instability along routes to Cameroon and Sudan restrict trade, fuel supply and state control outside Bangui. China and other foreign operators may expand commercial engagement, but logistics remain dependent on external security and transit states.

highlights: Oil revenues anchor a centralized state

frictionVectors.title: Oil dependence and external operators
frictionVectors.details: Chad's fiscal and political system remains heavily dependent on oil, with production, export routes and technical capacity tied to foreign companies and regional infrastructure. Limited diversification leaves sovereign control vulnerable to price shifts and contract asymmetries.

frictionVectors.title: Sudan spillover and security partnerships
frictionVectors.details: The war in Sudan places pressure on eastern borders through refugee flows, arms trafficking and cross-border armed networks. As Western military engagement changes, N'Djamena is balancing relations with France, Gulf actors, Russia and regional partners to preserve regime security.

frictionVectors.title: Mayotte and Maritime Access
frictionVectors.details: The unresolved dispute with France over Mayotte remains the central sovereignty issue, affecting migration policy, maritime jurisdiction, and access to surrounding fisheries.

frictionVectors.title: External Financing Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Comoros relies heavily on remittances and external partners, leaving infrastructure and energy projects vulnerable to shifting French, Gulf, and Chinese priorities.

frictionVectors.title: Mineral Supply-Chain Competition
frictionVectors.details: Cobalt, copper, and other critical minerals attract intense competition from Chinese, Western, and regional actors, while weak oversight limits Kinshasa's ability to capture full value.

frictionVectors.title: Eastern Security and Border Interference
frictionVectors.details: Conflict involving armed groups and alleged external support continues to weaken territorial control in the east and threatens mining corridors, transport infrastructure, and civilian access to resources.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Oil remains the backbone of public finance, exposing national resource security to price shocks and limiting diversification beyond hydrocarbons.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and Infrastructure Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed infrastructure and financing have expanded connectivity but also increase dependence on external contractors, creditors, and commodity-linked repayment structures.

frictionVectors.title: Cocoa and Critical Commodity Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Côte d'Ivoire is improving domestic processing and fiscal capture, but producer incomes and national resilience remain exposed to international cocoa prices and foreign buyers.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic Partner Competition
frictionVectors.details: French, Chinese, Gulf, and Western partners are competing for ports, energy, transport, and digital infrastructure, creating leverage opportunities but also long-term dependency risks.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Military Presence
frictionVectors.details: Djibouti monetizes its position beside the Bab el-Mandeb through multiple foreign military facilities, but the concentration of external security interests constrains independent strategic maneuver.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Debt Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Port infrastructure and corridor projects generate vital revenue while leaving the state exposed to competition among China, Gulf investors, Western partners, and creditors over logistics assets.

highlights: Suez corridor remains a strategic revenue lifeline
Gulf and IMF financing deepen external leverage

frictionVectors.title: Debt and asset-sale pressure
frictionVectors.details: Heavy financing needs have increased reliance on Gulf capital, multilateral lenders, and state-asset monetization. This can constrain independent control over strategic infrastructure and industrial policy.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea and Nile security
frictionVectors.details: Shipping disruption around the Red Sea threatens Suez revenues, while unresolved Nile-water tensions with Ethiopia remain a core sovereignty concern.

highlights: Hydrocarbon output declines accelerate diversification pressure
Chinese-backed infrastructure remains central to state capacity

frictionVectors.title: Oil-sector dependence
frictionVectors.details: Falling petroleum production and limited economic diversification leave public finances exposed to external energy firms, opaque contracting, and volatile global prices.

frictionVectors.title: Chinese infrastructure leverage
frictionVectors.details: Chinese financing and construction have expanded roads, ports, and public facilities, but debt exposure and contractor dependence reduce domestic bargaining power.

highlights: Strategic Red Sea geography raises external attention
Mining revenues remain constrained by isolation and sanctions risk

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea militarization
frictionVectors.details: The coastline’s proximity to major shipping routes and regional conflicts invites pressure from Gulf, Turkish, and Western actors. Asmara remains highly protective of access and security sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Mining and labor scrutiny
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-linked mining projects provide scarce hard currency but face persistent allegations over labor conditions, transparency, and state control of revenues.

highlights: South African trade access anchors the economy
Royal control and fiscal dependence limit policy autonomy

frictionVectors.title: South African dependency
frictionVectors.details: Most trade, transport links, energy flows, and remittances are tied to South Africa and the Southern African regional market. Disruptions there would quickly affect Eswatini’s fiscal and supply security.

frictionVectors.title: Political legitimacy pressure
frictionVectors.details: Political restrictions and concentrated control over land and economic assets generate domestic friction, complicating efforts to attract diversified investment without external conditionality.

highlights: GERD strengthens national control over energy strategy
Debt, conflict, and port dependence constrain sovereignty

frictionVectors.title: Nile and GERD diplomacy
frictionVectors.details: The dam improves Ethiopia’s leverage over electricity and development planning but continues to generate acute tensions with Egypt and Sudan over filling, operations, and downstream guarantees.

frictionVectors.title: Port-access vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Landlocked Ethiopia remains dependent on Djibouti and other external corridors for most maritime trade. Negotiations over Red Sea access are strategically sensitive and vulnerable to regional rivalry.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign concession renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: Authorities are pressing international mining and oil operators for greater domestic processing, revenue capture, and local content. The policy improves bargaining leverage but risks investor caution and project delays.

frictionVectors.title: Port and rail dependency
frictionVectors.details: Export corridors and mineral logistics remain dependent on foreign capital, contractors, and technical expertise. Control over transport infrastructure is central to whether Gabon converts resource wealth into sovereign industrial capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Illegal and opaque fishing
frictionVectors.details: Foreign industrial fleets and weak monitoring continue to threaten coastal livelihoods and state control over fisheries. Enforcement capacity and licensing transparency remain persistent vulnerabilities.

frictionVectors.title: Senegalese economic dependence
frictionVectors.details: Trade, transport, energy links, and regional security cooperation with Senegal are essential but constrain policy autonomy. Border and transit frictions can quickly affect food and fuel security.

highlights: Gold and oil governance under scrutiny

frictionVectors.title: Gold-sector leakage
frictionVectors.details: Smuggling, informal production, and environmental damage reduce public capture from gold despite strong national production. Efforts to formalize artisanal mining and tighten buying controls face entrenched commercial networks.

frictionVectors.title: External financing constraints
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and IMF-linked reforms limit short-term policy space while external creditors and investors retain influence over fiscal and infrastructure choices. Maintaining domestic ownership of strategic assets remains politically sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: Simandou external consortium power
frictionVectors.details: The Simandou iron-ore project brings major infrastructure and revenue potential but relies heavily on foreign capital, operators, and export logistics. The state must prevent enclave development and secure credible local-content and fiscal terms.

frictionVectors.title: Bauxite corridor dependence
frictionVectors.details: Guinea's economy remains tied to foreign mining houses, port capacity, and commodity demand. Expansion without stronger domestic processing and environmental safeguards risks deepening extraction without broad-based sovereignty gains.

highlights: Fragile state control over natural assets
Cashew and fisheries remain externally exposed

frictionVectors.title: Opaque fisheries access
frictionVectors.details: Limited maritime surveillance and weak institutions leave fisheries vulnerable to foreign overexploitation and underreported licensing revenue. This directly undermines food security and public finances.

frictionVectors.title: Commodity-chain dependence
frictionVectors.details: Cashew exports remain dominated by external buyers and constrained by inadequate roads, storage, and processing capacity. Foreign commercial influence is strongest where the state lacks the infrastructure to retain value domestically.

highlights: Geothermal expansion strengthens domestic energy autonomy
Debt pressure limits infrastructure bargaining power

frictionVectors.title: EXTERNAL DEBT LEVERAGE
frictionVectors.details: Debt-servicing pressures and reliance on multilateral lenders constrain Nairobi's freedom to set infrastructure and development priorities. Chinese-linked and Western-backed projects remain important but increasingly face stricter scrutiny.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND CORRIDOR COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: Competition among foreign investors around Mombasa, Lamu, and regional transport corridors creates strategic leverage over Kenya's trade routes. Regional instability also raises security and operating costs.

highlights: Water exports deepen dependence on South Africa
Diamond sector offers revenue but limited autonomy

frictionVectors.title: WATER SOVEREIGNTY
frictionVectors.details: The Lesotho Highlands Water Project provides vital revenue and infrastructure, but binds national finances and water policy closely to South Africa. Project delays, cost overruns, and security concerns remain politically sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: MINING CONCESSION DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-owned diamond operations dominate a narrow export base, leaving the state exposed to commodity cycles and limited domestic value addition. Weak fiscal capacity reduces leverage in negotiating long-term concessions.

highlights: Iron ore revival attracts major concession capital
Ports and land concessions test state control

frictionVectors.title: IRON ORE CONCESSIONS
frictionVectors.details: Large foreign mining concessions are central to Liberia's growth strategy but generate recurring concerns over taxation, local employment, environmental obligations, and domestic processing. The state remains dependent on external operators for capital and logistics.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND RAIL ACCESS
frictionVectors.details: Mining-linked rail and port infrastructure can improve national connectivity while also locking strategic corridors into concession-specific export models. Monrovia's limited logistics capacity weakens Liberia's negotiating position.

highlights: Oil wealth remains divided among rival power centers
Foreign actors compete over energy infrastructure

frictionVectors.title: FRAGMENTED OIL GOVERNANCE
frictionVectors.details: Competing institutions, armed groups, and regional authorities continue to threaten unified control of production, budgets, and export terminals. Periodic blockades can rapidly convert political disputes into national revenue crises.

frictionVectors.title: EXTERNAL SECURITY AND ENERGY LEVERAGE
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, Russia, Gulf states, Egypt, and European actors retain influence through security ties, contracts, and energy interests. Foreign-backed networks complicate efforts to centralize infrastructure protection and sovereign decision-making.

highlights: Critical-mineral exports outpace domestic value addition

frictionVectors.title: MINERAL PROJECT DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Nickel, cobalt, ilmenite, and other mineral projects are dominated by foreign capital and export infrastructure, limiting Madagascar's ability to capture downstream value. Fiscal and environmental disputes continue to shape public attitudes toward major concessions.

frictionVectors.title: POWER AND LOGISTICS BOTTLENECKS
frictionVectors.details: Chronic electricity shortages, weak roads, and constrained ports leave the country dependent on external project operators for essential infrastructure. This reduces bargaining power when negotiating mining, energy, and transport agreements.

frictionVectors.title: Critical Minerals Bargaining
frictionVectors.details: Malawi is seeking foreign capital for uranium, rare-earth and graphite projects while trying to secure stronger local processing and fiscal terms. Limited negotiating capacity risks leaving the country dependent on external operators and commodity cycles.

frictionVectors.title: Energy and Fuel Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chronic electricity shortages and imported fuel constrain industrial sovereignty. Regional power links and private investment are expanding options, but financing and foreign-exchange shortages remain major bottlenecks.

frictionVectors.title: Gold Contract Renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The junta is pressing foreign mining companies for larger state shares, higher revenues and tighter control over gold exports. The strategy may improve fiscal capture but risks arbitration, delayed investment and operational disruption.

frictionVectors.title: Russian Security Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Mali relies increasingly on Russian-linked security personnel and equipment as relations with Western partners deteriorate. This reduces outside political leverage in the short term but increases dependence on a single external security supplier.

frictionVectors.title: GTA Gas Governance
frictionVectors.details: The Greater Tortue Ahmeyim project offers Mauritania new export revenue and strategic weight, but offshore infrastructure and marketing remain tied to foreign energy companies and regional partners. Revenue transparency and domestic value capture are central sovereignty tests.

frictionVectors.title: Mining and Infrastructure Concentration
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore and prospective green-hydrogen projects require large foreign-backed rail, port and power investments. Concentrated ownership and weak downstream processing could limit local gains while increasing exposure to commodity and geopolitical competition.

frictionVectors.title: Chagos and Indian Ocean Alignment
frictionVectors.details: The Chagos settlement and management of Diego Garcia remain strategically sensitive, balancing Mauritian sovereignty claims with British-American security interests. Port access, maritime surveillance and regional alignment will remain externally contested.

frictionVectors.title: External Economic Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius retains strong institutional control but remains vulnerable to foreign demand in tourism, finance and seafood. Regulatory pressure from major markets and competition over Indian Ocean connectivity could narrow policy autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara Resource Politics
frictionVectors.details: Phosphates, fisheries, renewables and port development in Western Sahara remain subject to legal and diplomatic contestation. Morocco's control is strengthened by investment and foreign partnerships, but recognition and consent disputes continue to generate external pressure.

frictionVectors.title: Water and Energy Security
frictionVectors.details: Morocco is expanding desalination, renewables and interconnections to reduce dependence on imported energy and climate-stressed water supplies. Large projects still rely on foreign technology, capital and long-term offtake agreements.

highlights: Cabo Delgado insurgency constrains LNG sovereignty
Maputo balances foreign capital with local-content demands

frictionVectors.title: LNG Security and Project Delays
frictionVectors.details: Insurgency and military-security dependence have delayed major offshore gas development, leaving Mozambique reliant on foreign operators and external security support.

frictionVectors.title: Resource-Corridor Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Coal, gas, and logistics corridors remain heavily shaped by multinational finance and neighboring transit infrastructure, limiting domestic leverage over value capture.

highlights: Green hydrogen ambitions test state capacity

frictionVectors.title: Oil and Uranium Partnership Terms
frictionVectors.details: Recent offshore oil discoveries and established uranium production are attracting major foreign capital, intensifying debate over taxation, ownership, and domestic processing.

frictionVectors.title: Green Hydrogen Infrastructure Gap
frictionVectors.details: Large hydrogen projects depend on external technology, financing, and export infrastructure, creating risks that Namibia remains primarily a low-value energy supplier.

highlights: Junta asserts control over uranium and oil policy

frictionVectors.title: Security Partnership Realignment
frictionVectors.details: The military government has reduced Western security ties and expanded cooperation with Russia, but persistent jihadist violence limits effective control of resource-producing areas.

frictionVectors.title: Export-Corridor Vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Sanctions, border tensions, and instability around oil-export routes constrain Niger's ability to convert formal resource sovereignty into reliable revenue.

frictionVectors.title: Oil Theft and Pipeline Insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Sabotage, theft, and aging infrastructure continue to reduce state capture of petroleum value while complicating partnerships with international oil companies.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Capital and Refining Dependence
frictionVectors.details: New domestic refining capacity strengthens sovereignty, but upstream investment, technical services, and energy infrastructure remain substantially dependent on foreign firms and finance.

highlights: Security influence extends across eastern Congo

frictionVectors.title: Eastern Congo Mineral Supply Chains
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda faces sustained international accusations that its regional security role facilitates illicit mineral flows, exposing Kigali to sanctions and diplomatic pressure.

frictionVectors.title: External Aid and Strategic Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Strong state coordination attracts investment and aid, but dependence on external markets, donors, and security relationships limits fully autonomous resource governance.

frictionVectors.title: OFFSHORE EXPLORATION UNCERTAINTY
frictionVectors.details: Prospective Gulf of Guinea blocks attract foreign interest, but limited discoveries, financing constraints, and weak state capacity have prevented meaningful petroleum sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: FISHERIES AND MARITIME SURVEILLANCE
frictionVectors.details: São Tomé depends on external partners for maritime monitoring while seeking to protect fisheries and its wider maritime zone from foreign vessels.

highlights: New oil and gas era begins

frictionVectors.title: CONTRACT RENEGOTIATION
frictionVectors.details: Dakar is pressing for greater state participation and revised terms in hydrocarbon projects, creating tension with international operators and lenders while production ramps up.

frictionVectors.title: CROSS-BORDER GAS GOVERNANCE
frictionVectors.details: The Greater Tortue Ahmeyim project with Mauritania requires sustained coordination over revenue, infrastructure, and operational control in shared offshore waters.

frictionVectors.title: FOREIGN FISHING ACCESS
frictionVectors.details: Seychelles retains regulatory authority over its waters but remains exposed to bargaining pressure from distant-water fleets and tuna-processing interests.

frictionVectors.title: EXTERNAL MARITIME INFRASTRUCTURE
frictionVectors.details: Indian and other international security partnerships improve surveillance capacity, but competition among outside powers raises sovereignty sensitivities around ports and strategic islands.

frictionVectors.title: FOREIGN MINING CONTROL
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore, rutile, and other mineral projects rely heavily on foreign capital and operators, limiting domestic value capture despite government efforts to improve licensing and revenue oversight.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND RAIL DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Mineral export corridors and port infrastructure tie national revenue prospects to external companies, creating disputes over land, environmental impacts, and contract transparency.

frictionVectors.title: TURKISH OFFSHORE ENERGY ROLE
frictionVectors.details: Turkey's expanding energy and maritime-security partnership offers Somalia technical capacity but raises scrutiny over licensing terms, revenue sharing, and long-term control of offshore resources.

frictionVectors.title: FEDERAL AND REGIONAL SOVEREIGNTY
frictionVectors.details: Disputes among the federal government, member states, and Somaliland complicate petroleum licensing, port access, and maritime claims while insecurity restricts effective state control.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Ownership and Beneficiation
frictionVectors.details: South Africa is seeking greater domestic value capture from platinum, manganese and other critical minerals while remaining dependent on foreign capital, technology and export markets.

frictionVectors.title: Electricity and Port Bottlenecks
frictionVectors.details: Grid instability and constrained freight rail and ports weaken sovereign control over mineral supply chains and increase reliance on private operators and external investment.

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline Dependence on Sudan
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan’s oil exports rely on infrastructure crossing conflict-affected Sudan, leaving revenue, production and export access vulnerable to external leverage and disruption.

frictionVectors.title: Elite and Foreign Resource Competition
frictionVectors.details: Armed factions, political elites and foreign commercial actors compete over oil and other natural resources, limiting transparent state control and sustaining fiscal fragility.

frictionVectors.title: Gold Networks and External Patrons
frictionVectors.details: Competing wartime authorities and outside networks benefit from informal gold channels, diverting resource revenue and weakening national institutions.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea Infrastructure Rivalry
frictionVectors.details: Port access, military partnerships and logistics concessions on the Red Sea are increasingly entangled with regional and global competition, reducing Sudan’s autonomous bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-Minerals Investment Terms
frictionVectors.details: Tanzania is tightening local-processing and revenue expectations for graphite, nickel and other minerals while competing for investment from foreign mining and industrial groups.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Rail Geopolitics
frictionVectors.details: Development of Dar es Salaam-linked rail and port corridors is expanding national leverage but also deepening exposure to competing Chinese, Gulf, Indian and Western financing interests.

frictionVectors.title: Port-Centered External Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Port of Lomé strengthens Togo’s regional role, but operations, finance and trade flows remain heavily shaped by foreign shipping, logistics and commercial interests.

frictionVectors.title: Phosphate Governance
frictionVectors.details: Phosphate remains strategically important, yet limited downstream processing and reliance on external technology and markets constrain domestic value capture.

frictionVectors.title: EU migration and financing pressure
frictionVectors.details: European financial support and trade access remain closely tied to migration cooperation, giving Brussels substantial leverage over Tunisian policy. Tunisia resists being treated as an external border-management platform while facing acute fiscal constraints.

frictionVectors.title: Gas and power vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Declining domestic energy output and reliance on Algerian gas and imported fuels limit sovereign control over electricity security. Delays in renewable investment and grid modernization keep exposure elevated.

highlights: Oil corridor advances amid sovereignty concerns

frictionVectors.title: EACOP financing and sanctions
frictionVectors.details: The East African Crude Oil Pipeline remains a major sovereignty project for Kampala but faces Western criticism, financing restrictions, and environmental litigation. Uganda is increasingly dependent on a narrower group of Gulf, Chinese, and regional partners to advance the project.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure-for-access bargaining
frictionVectors.details: Chinese and Gulf-linked capital supports transport, energy, and extractive infrastructure while creating long-term repayment and concession risks. Uganda is balancing diversification of partners against reduced transparency and potential loss of bargaining power.

highlights: Debt restructuring restores room to maneuver

frictionVectors.title: Critical minerals competition
frictionVectors.details: Zambia is using its copper and cobalt position to attract investment and promote local processing, but Chinese, Western, and Gulf-backed firms are competing for influence across the value chain. The central risk is that new capital expands production without transferring sufficient refining capacity or fiscal value.

frictionVectors.title: Rail and corridor dependence
frictionVectors.details: Copper exports remain vulnerable to bottlenecks on regional rail and road corridors through Tanzania, Zimbabwe, and the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Corridor diversification improves bargaining power but requires substantial external financing and coordination.

frictionVectors.title: Lithium and platinum value capture
frictionVectors.details: Zimbabwe is seeking domestic beneficiation and tighter control over lithium exports, yet mining development remains dependent on foreign capital, technology, and market access. Chinese firms retain a strong position, while Western and regional investors remain cautious because of sanctions and regulatory uncertainty.

frictionVectors.title: Power and currency fragility
frictionVectors.details: Electricity shortages and dependence on imported power undermine mining expansion and broader industrial sovereignty. Persistent currency instability encourages dollarization and limits the government's ability to manage resource revenues through a stable domestic financial system.
